Drag
drăg
n. (a dragnet, the great net drawn along the sea bottom; in Habakkuk, the tackle a conqueror worships)
From Old English dragan, to draw. The drag of Habakkuk is a fishing implement — the heavy net dragged through the water — and the prophet makes it the idol of an empire.

Biblical Definition

Habakkuk watches the Chaldean sweep the nations up like fish and describes it in three implements: “They take up all of them with the angle, they catch them in their net, and gather them in their drag: therefore they rejoice and are glad” (Hab 1:15). Then comes the sentence that names the sin of every conqueror and every self-made man: “Therefore they sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag; because by them their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous” (Hab 1:16). The empire does not worship a god; it worships its own tackle. And the prophet has already asked what makes it possible: God has made men “as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them” (Hab 1:14). The answer given to Habakkuk's complaint is not an explanation of the Chaldean but a rule for the righteous: “Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith” (Hab 2:4) — the verse Paul takes up three times and Luther after him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives drag as a net drawn along the bottom of the water; also a hook or grapple for drawing under water; and to drag as to pull or haul along the ground by main force.

expand to see more

DRAG, v.t. To pull; to haul; to draw along the ground by main force.

2. To draw along slowly or heavily; to draw any thing burdensome.

DRAG, n. A net drawn along the bottom of the water.

They burn incense unto their drag. Hab. i.

Key Scripture

Hab 1:15 — "They take up all of them with the angle, they catch them in their net, and gather them in their drag: therefore they rejoice and are glad."

Hab 1:16 — "Therefore they sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag; because by them their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous."

Hab 1:14 — "And makest men as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them?"

Hab 2:4 — "Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith."

Modern Corruption

Idolatry is imagined as bowing to a carved figure, when Habakkuk's conqueror burns incense to the instrument of his own success and never leaves the harbour.

expand to see more

Habakkuk 1:16 is the sharpest definition of practical idolatry in the prophets, and it involves no image at all. The Chaldean sacrifices to his net. He has looked at the machinery by which he prospered — his army, his method, his fleet — and concluded that it is what fed him, and so his devotion goes there. The tell is given in the same verse: because by them their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous. Whatever a man credits for his fatness gets his incense. In our own setting the drag is a business, a portfolio, a platform, a network of the right relationships, or a method of ministry; and the worship is not usually spoken. It shows in what a man will not risk, what he defends most fiercely, and what he assumes he cannot live without. Deuteronomy warned Israel against the identical sentence before they ever crossed Jordan: thou say in thine heart, My power and the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth.

The prophet's complaint in verse 14 is worth stating carefully because it is often quoted as though Scripture agreed with it. Habakkuk protests that God has made men as the fishes of the sea… that have no ruler over them — that is his charge, brought in prayer, and the whole book is God's answer to it. The answer does not deny the Chaldean's violence or excuse it; chapter two pronounces five woes on him. What it does is refuse to let the righteous man live by his reading of the times. The just shall live by his faith is given in the middle of an unanswered question, and Habakkuk ends singing that though the fig tree shall not blossom and there be no herd in the stalls, yet will he rejoice in the LORD. That is what a man has when his drag is empty, and it is the only thing worth having when it is full.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mikmereth (H4365), a fishing net or drag; cherem (H2764), a net; with zabach (H2076), to sacrifice, and qatar (H6999), to burn incense — both given to tackle.

expand to see more

Hebrew mikmereth (H4365) — a drag net; they burn incense unto their drag; Habakkuk 1:16.

Hebrew cherem (H2764) — a net; also, by a separate root, a devoted thing; Habakkuk 1:15.

Hebrew zabach (H2076) — to slaughter, to sacrifice; offered here to a fishing net; Habakkuk 1:16.

Hebrew emunah (H530) — steadfastness, faithfulness, faith; the just shall live by his faith; Habakkuk 2:4.

Greek sagene (G4522) — a dragnet; the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea; Matthew 13:47.

Usage

"“They gather them in their drag” — nations taken like fish."

"“They sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag” — idolatry with no image."

"“The just shall live by his faith” — the answer given while the question stood."
